title_en: The Signature of Closure: A Limitative Argument for Naturalism
The Concept of God in Early Nishida’s Philosophy
abstract: This study examines how Nishida Kitarō’s early philosophy redefines the concept of God within the framework of pure experience ( junsui keiken , 純粋経験). Reading An Inquiry into the Good (1911) alongside the Fragments on Pure Experience (1903–1912) and the Lectures on Religion (1913–1914), it traces how the concept of God develops from the logic of experience rather than from any transcendent domain. For Nishida, the religious demand arises from life’s inner need to unify the finite and the infinite; God, accordingly, is not a being among beings but the unifying activity ( tōitsu , 統一) through which knowing and being are one. Against the familiar picture of Nishida as a champion of immanence against a monolithic “Western dualism,” the study argues that his position is a non-dualism that refuses both the separation of theism and the fusion of monistic pantheism, and that his true target is the metaphysics of substance: a target contested within the Western tradition itself, as his endorsement of Nicholas of Cusa’s coincidentia oppositorum in the recently published (2020) autograph notebooks of the Lectures on Religion attests. On this reading, the early notion of God as unifying activity is the structural antecedent of absolute nothingness ( zettai mu , 絶対無): a unity that is no object of knowledge and no determinate thing, yet that by which all things are established, already, in all but name, the mature concept of place ( basho , 場所).

title_en: Divine commands and the problem of due promulgation
journal: International Journal for Philosophy of Religion
abstract: This paper develops a new argument against the existence of the Abrahamic God, understood as Supreme Lawgiver and Judge. Just law requires due promulgation: no one can be justly held accountable for laws they could not reasonably know. Yet not all rational agents can, with minimal conscientious reflection, discover the divine commands binding on them. The failure of conscience, natural law, and the sensus divinitatis to resolve this problem shows that due promulgation has not occurred. Because the Abrahamic God represents Himself in Abrahamic scriptures as a just lawgiver who holds rational agents accountable for commands he has adequately promulgated to them, this failure entails that He does not exist. Unlike the problems of evil or hiddenness, which turn on contested expectations, the promulgation argument shows that the Abrahamic God fails by his own standards, which also correspond to our core intuitions concerning justice.

title_en: The Logical Problem of Evil from a Paraconsistent Perspective
authors: Fabio Maia Bertato, Itala M. Loffredo D'Ottaviano
abstract: The logical problem of evil challenges the coherence of theism by claiming that the existence of an omnipotent, omniscient, and omnibenevolent God is incompatible with the presence of evil. Within classical logic, such an incompatibility would entail triviality, since any contradiction triggers the principle ex contradictione sequitur quodlibet. This paper investigates the problem by focusing on the logical relation between contradiction, triviality, and theological reasoning. It begins by examining the role played by explosion in classical logic and by tracing the historical development of non-explosive approaches to inconsistency, culminating in contemporary paraconsistent logics. Against this background, a first-order classical system is presented in which omnipotence, omniscience, and omnibenevolence are defined in a minimal but precise way and combined with the empirical premise that evil exists. It is shown that, under these assumptions, no contradiction follows, and thus the logical problem of evil does not succeed in its strongest classical form. At the same time, the analysis highlights the vulnerability of such classical solutions: once stronger theological assumptions are introduced, contradiction again threatens to trivialize the theory. The paper then argues that paraconsistent logic provides a robust framework for formal natural theology, allowing tensions between divine attributes and evil to be articulated without collapse.

title_en: Gnosticism as the Deep Structure of Modernity: A Philosophical-Anthropological and Political Analysis
authors: Melike Çelebi Özcan, Muhammet Caner Ilgaroğlu
abstract: This study examines modern humanity’s existential crisis and search for meaning from philosophical-anthropological and political perspectives by exploring structural parallels with ancient Gnostic cosmology. It argues that the existential void and chronic alienation arising from the dissolution of traditional theological frameworks cannot be adequately explained through purely sociological or empirical approaches. To illuminate the metaphysical dimensions of this crisis, the study brings Hegel’s, Marx’s, and Heidegger’s theories of alienation into dialogue with Eric Voegelin’s critique of the “Gnostic temptation” and the philosophical anthropology of Max Scheler, Arnold Gehlen, and Helmuth Plessner. Methodologically, it adopts a comparative-hermeneutic approach in which structural analysis serves as the primary comparative principle, while phenomenological analysis clarifies how alienation is experienced across different philosophical frameworks. Rather than positing historical, genealogical, or causal continuity between modernity and ancient Gnosticism, the study identifies structural correspondences in how human beings experience estrangement, interpret disorder, and imagine possibilities of liberation, reconciliation, or transformation. It argues that modern alienation exhibits a pattern analogous to the Gnostic myth of the soul’s estrangement within a flawed material world, while differing substantially in its ontological assumptions and responses. Thus, modernity reveals structural affinities with the Gnostic imagination without implying direct historical or doctrinal continuity.

title_en: The Price of Perfection: Moral Enhancement, Free Will, and the Limits of Technological Salvation
abstract: In 2017, Elon Musk stated that humans must augment their mental capabilities through the “merger of biological intelligence and machine intelligence” lest they risk becoming “house cats” to artificial intelligence. In 2024, he successfully implanted his “Neuralink” chip in a human patient. Now, while the idea of improving the human condition by integrating technology into the human body did not begin with Elon Musk, his tangible advancements in neural implants have shifted the ethical questions surrounding them from theoretical to practical. One particularly thorny application of this technology—one that raises both ethical and existential questions—is its use for moral enhancement. Ethically, we must consider whether it is good or bad to employ technology that ensures individuals act morally. Existentially, if human free will is expressed most meaningfully through moral choice, should we be willing to relinquish that freedom for the sake of social harmony, crime prevention, even world peace? Or must we accept a world marked by moral failure, violence, and injustice in order to preserve human autonomy? To address these questions, I examine contemporary philosophical debates surrounding moral enhancement and place them in dialogue with classical Jewish sources. For, as will be shown, Jewish thought offers a unique framework for addressing both the ethical permissibility of moral enhancement and the existential tension between free will and moral perfection. By juxtaposing cutting-edge neurotechnology with ancient moral anthropology, this paper invites a reassessment of what it means to be human in an age increasingly capable of reshaping human agency itself.

title_en: Substance and Emptiness: A Comparative Study of the “Absolute Being” in Kant’s Philosophy of Religion and Tathāgatagarbha–Dharmakāya Thought in the Ratnagotravibhāga
abstract: This article compares the concept of the “Absolute Being” in Kant’s philosophy of religion with tathāgatagarbha–dharmakāya thought in the Ratnagotravibhāga, focusing on their conceptual forms and philosophical functions. In the theoretical reason, Kant restricts the most real being to a transcendental ideal of pure reason and permits only its regulative use; in the practical reason, Kant grants the idea of God the legitimacy of rational faith by treating it as a moral postulate. By contrast, the Ratnagotravibhāga uses dharmakāya, tathāgatagarbha, and buddha-nature to explain the ground of sentient beings’ attainment of Buddhahood, and develops an emphatically affirmative soteriological discourse through the four qualities of “permanence, bliss, self, and purity” and the nine similes. The article argues that the two are not substantially the same kind of “absolute”. Kant’s “Absolute Being” has only the status of an idea and a postulate: critical philosophy denies theoretical knowledge of it without removing the personal determinations of the practical idea of God. Tathāgatagarbha–dharmakāya, for its part, must be understood within the limits imposed by dependent origination, no-self, and twofold emptiness. Even so, the two display a limited but identifiable functional correspondence insofar as both mark the limits of cognition, sustain the meaning of practice, and contribute to systematic unity. By submitting each position to the reciprocal scrutiny of Madhyamaka emptiness and Kantian critique, the article further argues that this correspondence is illuminating only when their ontological, epistemological, and soteriological differences are fully acknowledged. The tension between substance and emptiness is therefore not an opposition that can simply be dissolved; it is an occasion on which two traditions can disclose one another’s theoretical presuppositions and boundaries.

title_en: Defending Purpose Theory of Meaning: Meeting Koons’s New Euthyphro Dilemma
abstract: The recent surge of interest in the philosophical study of life’s meaning generated multiple challenges to a default, often taken-for-granted theistic position—Divine Purpose Theory (DPT). This paper defends DPT against Koons’s Euthyphro Dilemma (KED), which questions whether a purpose is meaningful because God assigned it or did God assign that purpose because it is meaningful. The first horn implies that God’s purpose is arbitrary, while the second horn renders God otiose in life’s meaning. Koons points out that the standard theistic response to KED fails because it generates asecond-order Euthyphro dilemma that remains unresolved. This paper first argues that we can resolve the second-order Euthyphro dilemma if we read Koons’s interlocutor—Alston—more charitably. Second, this paper shows how KED misses the target. While DPT is an account of life’s meaningfulness, KED is only about purposes’ meaningfulness. In addition, this paper also argues that KED, even as a challenge to an account of purposes’ meaningfulness, is a false dilemma. Last, this paper modifies KED into a version (Revised-KED) that specifically targets DPT as an account of life’s meaningfulness and argues that committing to the first horn of Revised-KED does not imply that God is arbitrary in God’s choice of purposes.

title_en: Atheism and the meaning of life
abstract: The editors introduce the special issue on atheism and the meaning of life, providing an overview of its scope and a concise summary of the contributions included in the issue.

title_en: Bridging the Ineffable: James Legge’s Theological Association of the Tao with God in His Translation of the Tao Te Ching
abstract: While James Legge’s 19th-century translation of the Tao Te Ching played a foundational role in the work’s Western reception, his explicit association of “Tao” (道) with the Christian “God” has often been dismissed reductively as missionary bias. That reading misses something. Legge’s theological framing was less an imposition of his fulfillment theology, his fierce advocacy for “Shang-Ti” (上帝) in the late Qing “Term Question” debates, and the institutional demands of Max Müller’s Sacred Books of the East series. Drawing on Bourdieu’s concept of habitus, Lefevere’s theory of patronage, and close reading of Legge’s translated text and its paratext, the paper reconstructs the logic of a strategy that was, in its own terms, coherent. The Tao-God association distorted the naturalistic and embodied character of Taoist thought in ways that took decades to correct. But the same framework that distorted also canonized: without Legge’s theological repackaging, the Tao Te Ching might have remained what it was before his intervention—a curiosity at the margins of Victorian learning.

title_en: Tajwīd as a Codified Discipline: An Analysis in Light of Avicenna’s Criteria for Science
abstract: Tajwīd was recognized as an ʿilm in classical Islamic scholarship, yet its epistemic status as a codified discipline has received comparatively little systematic examination. This study investigates whether tajwīd exhibits Avicenna’s structural criteria for science: a determinate subject matter (mawḍūʿ), foundational principles (mabādiʾ), and organized problems (masāʾil). The analysis finds that tajwīd takes the letters of the Qurʾān, insofar as they are realized in recitation, as its subject matter; rests on self-evident, inductive, transmitted, and normative principles; and organizes its problems around articulation points (makhārij), phonetic attributes (ṣifāt), phonetic interactions, including idghām, elongation (madd), pausing and resumption (waqf and ibtidāʾ), and recitational error (laḥn). Its aim is to preserve the transmitted verbal and recitational form of the Qurʾān and maintain the integrity between wording and meaning. Methodologically, the study employs qualitative conceptual and textual analysis conducted through a structural and functional analogical framework. It shows that tajwīd combines theoretical systematization with supervised practice through transmission, listening, recitation before a qualified teacher, repetition, and correction. This analysis contributes to existing scholarship by shifting attention from the individual rules and pedagogical transmission of tajwīd to its internal disciplinary architecture, and by showing how a transmission-based and practice-centered Qurʾānic discipline can be analyzed through a classical Islamic framework of scientific organization without being reduced to demonstrative science. The study concludes that tajwīd is not identical to a demonstrative science but can be characterized as a codified, normative, transmission-grounded, and practice-centered Qurʾānic discipline within the broader classical Islamic conception of ʿilm.

title_en: God-Nature and the Walpurgisnacht Motif in Goethe’s Faust: Religious Continuity and Contestation in Literary Form
abstract: Goethe’s three Walpurgisnacht scenes in Faust are usually separated as demonic spectacle, satirical intermezzo, and classical phantasmagoria. Read together, they form a poetic sequence interpreted through Goethe’s conception of God-Nature (Gott-Natur), a non-systematic conception of divinity as immanent in living, metamorphic nature. The sequence moves from the expansion and interruption of demonic freedom on the Brocken, through a reconciliation of natural powers announced but withheld in “Walpurgis Night’s Dream,” to the attempted poetic return of God-Nature in the Greek Fabelreich. Religious and mythic traditions are not treated as evidence of an intact pagan cult; they supply historically contested symbolic materials that Goethe reshapes to examine modern subjectivity. The ballad “The First Walpurgis Night” clarifies how conflict over pagan natural festivity contributed to the motif’s demonic imagery, while the dramatic scenes transform mountain festivity, fairy comedy, sacred healing, divine genealogy, and metamorphosis into tests of Faust’s relation to limit. Greek soil revives him, but his desire for Helen turns participation into possession. The sequence thus stages religious continuity and contestation within literary form: inherited symbols remain available, yet their capacity to restore a divine-natural order depends on whether the modern subject can receive rather than master them.

title_en: Redemption and the Church of St. John: Futurity and Narrative Philosophy from Schelling to Rosenzweig
abstract: This article attempts to sketch the conditions of ‘narrative philosophy’, an idea rooted in the philosophies of Friedrich Schelling and Franz Rosenzweig, insofar as it is both a historical philosophy and a messianic–eschatological utopianism. The two contradictory perspectives unite around the idea of narrativity and a shared idea of the future as incessantly deferred u-topos. The article examines Schelling’s late sketch of the ‘three ages of the church’ (Kirchenalter) and its origins in Schelling’s Ages of the World (Weltalter) project, before detailing Rosenzweig’s relationship to this philosophy, specifically his grafting of the triadic Kirchenalter into his own philosophy. The focus is on the structural affinity between Schelling and Rosenzweig, insofar as they both have established open-ended utopianism, or messianism, which lies concealed in their nonetheless ‘purely rational’ systems of philosophy. The article plots the course of the entanglement, while also bringing out the originality of the ‘narrative philosophical’ enterprise, which in both cases was never fully systematized. Schelling never completed—or else abandoned—the Weltalter, while Rosenzweig died young before he could expand his ‘New Thinking’ system, which was first introduced in the Star of Redemption (Stern der Erlösung). The article also attempts to show how this narrativity depends on both an aesthetic framework and a political vision.

title_en: Ontological Aspect Shift: Rethinking Maimonides’ Thirteen Principles as Existential Structures of Being-in-Creation
abstract: Debates over Maimonides’ Thirteen Principles (Ikkarim) have examined their doctrinal authority and contested reception. This article asks how their truth claims belong to halakhic existence. Its theoretical framework treats nature and creation as ontological determinations of worldhood constituted and stabilized through practice. Drawing on Wittgenstein’s aspect-seeing and phenomenological accounts of worldhood, it defines an Ontological Aspect Shift as a transformation in how the same empirical reality is disclosed and inhabited. Applying this framework through analyses of Maimonides’ primary texts and rabbinic sources, the article interprets the Ikkarim as theological formulations of the existential structures of being-in-creation. Halakhic practice constitutes this worldhood; doctrine articulates its structures through claims concerning transcendence, revelation, judgment, and fulfillment. The argument distinguishes the normative priority of command, the constitutive primacy of practice, and the explicative and critical function of doctrine. Emunah is reconstructed as enacted receptivity while its cognitive uses retain their validity. This account concerns worldhood without making theological truth a product of practice. Its contribution is to explain how doctrinal affirmation participates in constituting and critically articulating a commanded way of inhabiting the world. The reading preserves Maimonides’ doctrinal demands while advancing an interpretation of their existential function that he does not himself formulate.

title_en: The Last Sartre: a Dawning at Dusk
Evil as attempted closure: Kierkegaard on selfhood, freedom, and faith
journal: International Journal for Philosophy of Religion

title_en: Does God have qualia? Some arguments in favour of the existence of divine qualia
abstract: Does God have qualia, does He know the ‘what it is like’ character of experiences? The questions run deep into the metaphysics of God as they concern concepts that most traditional theists accept with regard to God: that He is personal, loving, omniscient, omnipotent, and created the world ex nihilo . Building upon these concepts, I present four arguments in favour of the existence of divine qualia. Positing divine qualia may seem incompatible with divine simplicity, a tenet of classical theism, and the problem of emotions unworthy of God also may arise. I argue that the difficulties regarding simplicity do not stem from the existence of divine qualia per se but are related to difficulties already established in relation to simplicity. As for emotions unworthy of God, I try to show how a careful distinction between personal perspectives can offer a solution.

title_en: Life’s meaning and transcendence
abstract: This paper argues that the contemporary shift from the meaning of life to meaning in life reflects not a rejection of transcendence but a transformation in its structure. It distinguishes between absolute transcendence, which locates meaning within a comprehensive horizon beyond the situated subject, and immanent transcendence, which understands transcendence as the inexhaustibility of lived experience and interpretation. The former tends towards a third-person perspective and risks displacing the subject as the locus of meaning. The latter preserves the first-person perspective and grounds meaning in the subject’s relation to experiences, actions, and events that exceed its control. This shift also challenges the primacy of narrative identity: while narratives render actions intelligible, events reveal a more fundamental, pre-reflective dimension of subjectivity, identified here as the minimal self. Drawing on Taoist and Buddhist perspectives, particularly the concept of śūnyatā, the paper argues that meaning in life emerges through participation in a relational reality rather than through the fulfilment of an externally given purpose. Transcendence thus becomes an immanent feature of lived existence.

title_en: Are there substance dualist solutions to the non-identity problem?
journal: International Journal for Philosophy of Religion

title_en: God Without Theology and Theology Without God—Talmudic and Midrashic Ways of Stanislaw Lem’s Theological Thinking
abstract: This article examines, through a theological lens, the narrative landscape of Stanisław Lem—the Polish thinker and visionary author who died in 2006, leaving behind an indelible legacy in science fiction, exemplified by masterworks such as Solaris. The article begins by establishing the context, particularly focusing on the timeline of Lem’s fiction and the role of science within his narrative works. The core of the article is devoted to the concept of God and the related issue of theological thinking in Lem’s narratives. It is divided into two sections: the first explores Lem’s conception of God and theology, while the second analyses his approach to theological thinking. My intention is to argue that his theological methodology and conception of God exhibit characteristics akin to those found in Talmudic and Midrashic traditions. The text concludes with a reflection on faith from the Lemological perspective.

title_en: Gratitude to God in the Face of Adversity and Illness in Christianity and Islam
abstract: The conventional understanding of gratitude assumes that feeling grateful is reserved for joyous times. However, gratefulness during severe adversity is also documented. This paper focuses on this second phenomenon, examining experiences of gratitude toward God among Christian and Muslim parents of critically ill or disabled children. The ethnographic literature on this topic remains scarce. The goal of this paper is to read the few details this ethnographic literature offers in conjunction with Christian and Muslim theology on gratitude and adversity. Such an interpretive exercise sets out the theological resources these believers may draw upon. Our analysis reveals that reasons for their gratitude fall into two main categories: feeling grateful toward God despite adversity, or because of adversity. The essay compares these experiences in Christianity and Islam to highlight those key conceptual differences that emerge from the material. It also holds that the experience of gratitude towards God under conditions of suffering might partly destabilize the conventional philosophical model of gratitude. Overall, the material surveyed maps the range of meanings illness holds for some Christian and Muslim parents, offering valuable insights not only to theologians and philosophers of religion, but also to clinicians and chaplains.

title_en: Meaning, desire, and the limits of atheism
abstract: This paper defends a theistic framing of the problem of life’s meaning, albeit one which is intended to be compatible with a kind of naturalism. It makes explicit the significance of desire for an understanding of the issues at hand and draws out some implications for the question of the limits of atheism.

title_en: The human project or what difference would God make?
abstract: Many people believe that, without any God or something similarly ‘transcendent’, human life would be meaningless. I oppose this position. In its most popular form, it supposes that meaning accrues because our mundane life is merely a prelude – a time of trial, to decide the character of our life in the hereafter. When probed, this approach involves a number of implausible corollaries. More abstract approaches suggest that meaningfulness results from human contributions to a larger project, the fulfilment of some divine (or transcendent) scheme for the universe. That idea is more promising, but it fails to recognize the possibility of a larger – ‘human’ – project to which our lives may also contribute, and that from such contributions can arise significance. This possibility is suggested by John Dewey, and traces of it can be found in a number of insightful poets, Herbert, Wordsworth, and Whitman. Finally, I rebut the thought that, without something transcendent, there can be no values.

David Baggett and Jerry L. Walls, The Good, the Right, and the Real: Is Value a Fact? (New York: Oxford University Press, 2026). Pp. xxii + 304 (pbk). ISBN 9780197607138
Robert MacSwain, Saints as Divine Evidence: The Hagiological Argument for the Existence of God (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2025). pp. xviii + 295. £95.00(Hbk). ISBN 9781009653190.
Life After Death
Quantised Spacetime and the Case against Actual Infinities
The Value of Becoming Actual: Antinatalism, Cosmic Meaning, and Ontological Natal Permissibilism
authors: Ana Maria Correa Moreira da Silva, Leandro Prade Nadaletti
abstract: David Benatar’s antinatalism holds that coming into existence is always a harm and that procreation is therefore morally impermissible. This article develops a non-theistic alternative to a recent supernaturalist response to Benatar offered by Wakeman and Launonen. It defends ontological natal permissibilism: the view that actualizing a possible person as a perspectival subject is a defeasible prima facie good, and that this good can contribute to the moral permissibility of procreation when the expected conditions of life do not defeat it. The argument does not defend demographic pronatalism, a duty to reproduce, or the maximization of births. It instead challenges the priority Benatar gives to harm-avoidance by arguing that non-existence is not peace, protection, or safety, but the absence of a subject. Drawing on debates over cosmic meaning, Christian universalism, eternalism, and the Block Universe, the article distinguishes between physical and perspectival permanence. Mere inscription in spacetime does not generate value, since stones, collisions, and horrors also occur. Value arises when actuality includes conscious relation to reality, embodied presence, and world-contact. Ontological joy names the non-hedonic value of becoming actual as a possible perspective. Extreme suffering may defeat procreative permissibility, but it does not establish that birth is always only the imposition of harm.

title_en: Atheism, evolution, and meaning
abstract: In this paper, I argue that meaning of the main kinds associated with human life can be described and illuminatingly discussed by atheists who reject all things religious and embrace evolution. Indeed, by considering the different forms evolution can take and with sensitivity to how distinctive meaning-related facts emerge at different stages of macroscale human development and also to the fact that meaning itself evolves, atheists are in a position to show that the evolutionary considerations available to them, rather than an obstacle to a robust and satisfying account of meaning, can be its source.

title_en: Reconciling feminist critiques and classic theories of atonement
abstract: Work on atonement is fractured around how to respond to feminist critiques of classic atonement theories (such as satisfaction, moral exemplar, and penal substitution theories). Feminist and womanist scholars have levelled various critiques of these theories: the theories glorify sadomasochistic suffering, they encourage passivity in the face of suffering, and they are complicit in the oppression, victimization, and disempowerment of women in part because they legitimize patterns of oppression. Defenders of the classic theories have given various replies to these critiques, but these replies leave many feeling the heart of the critiques hasn’t really been addressed. In this paper, I aim to mend this fracture. I believe there is wisdom and insight on both sides of this dispute and that reflecting more carefully on a certain strand of feminist critique will present tools for mending. I develop a version of a feminist critique inspired by comments in several feminist critics of atonement theories – most notably Elizabeth Schussler Fiorenza. According to the critique I develop, the classic theories, together with Christian moral norms to imitate Christ, imply some version of the problematic attitudes mentioned above. This critique avoids the main objections to other feminist critiques. I then examine the notion of imitation and argue that, properly understood, the norm of imitating Christ (together with the classic atonement theories) does not have the problematic implications. Indeed, the norm and classic theories imply that imitating Christ by aiming at reconciliation among people requires rejecting the problematic attitudes.

title_en: Religious antinatalism: a rare breed
abstract: This article examines the relationship between religion and antinatalism – the view that it is wrong to create new sentient beings. Many people reject antinatalism on religious grounds. In this paper, I respond to such a rejection. First, I argue that antinatalism is not logically incompatible with theism. Second, I consider the pronatalist features of some religious traditions – those of Judaism, Christianity, Islam, and Buddhism. These include religious injunctions to procreate, imitatio Dei , and preservation of the religious community. I also show the limits of these pronatalist features. Third, I provide some examples of religious antinatalist thinking in the four surveyed religions. Finally, I say something about why many religions should be more antinatalist than they are. I do this by showing how central concepts – such as reducing suffering in Buddhism and original sin and hell in Christianity – provide compelling support for antinatalism.

title_en: A Review of the Functions and Properties of the Bhavaṅga-Citta: Reply to Sean Smith
Divine simplicity as symmetric parthood
abstract: Taken at face value, the doctrine of divine simplicity (DDS) says that God lacks proper parts, but the doctrine is also often formulated as a thesis identifying God with all his parts. The two formulations are not generally equivalent – on some plausible mereological theories, something can lack proper parts by being a part of all its (possibly distinct) parts. Thus, the DDS can be alternatively formulated as a thesis saying that God is part of all his parts – call this the symmetry formulation. The symmetry formulation is viable as a thesis about God’s relation to his attributes, because instantiation can plausibly be modelled as parthood. Moreover, the symmetry formulation retains the usual motivations for divine simplicity coming from the doctrines of aseity, transcendence, immutability, and unity. The symmetry formulation also addresses common objections to divine simplicity regarding distinctness in God’s attributes and those coming from modal collapse arguments.

title_en: Thibodeau and the Horrendous Deeds Objection: A Reply
Getting lost with the Mentaculus: Linford, the second law of thermodynamics, and cosmological arguments
journal: International Journal for Philosophy of Religion
